screens.title: Tracing Distributed Systems with Cloud Trace
screens.narratorSegment: Distributed tracing gives you a single, end-to-end view of a user request that traverses many services. In practice, tracing helps you answer concrete operational questions: which service introduced latency, where did an error originate, and what path did a transaction follow? In this lesson you will learn the core trace concepts—trace, span, context propagation—how to instrument code using OpenTelemetry or OpenCensus, and how to use the Cloud Trace console to inspect waterfall diagrams and span attributes. We'll walk through a hands-on Python example with two small services that simulate a validation and processing flow. You will also learn how to enrich traces with custom spans and annotations and the trade-offs around sampling and attribute cardinality. As you watch, think about a scenario from your applications where a single user action touches multiple services. Tracing will help you connect that activity into one coherent story so you can locate bottlenecks and understand error propagation. At the end of this chapter you'll know what to instrument, how to read traces, and how to avoid common propagation mistakes.

Module 12 › Chapter 12.3 › Tracing Distributed Systems
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Tracing Distributed Systems with Cloud Trace

Learn how traces and spans reveal the path of a user request through microservices, how to instrument code using OpenTelemetry, and how to analyze traces in the Cloud Trace console to find latency and errors.

In this lesson
  • Core trace concepts: trace, span, propagation.
  • Instrument with OpenTelemetry and export to Cloud Trace.
  • Analyze waterfall diagrams and correlate traces with logs and metrics.
Explore Key Topics
Instrumentation
Use OpenTelemetry/OpenCensus to generate spans and propagate context automatically.
Analysis
Waterfall diagrams show span durations and help locate latency bottlenecks.
Correlation
Attach trace IDs to logs and metrics to get a unified view of incidents.
Concept visual
E-commerce request flow
User → Auth → Product → Payment. Each step becomes a span in a trace; combined they show the full journey and timings.
Why this matters
When an order fails or slows down, a single trace can show which service produced the error and how latency propagated, saving time over manual log inspection across services.
Hands-on preview
You will run two small Python services instrumented with OpenTelemetry, generate traces by making requests, and inspect the Cloud Trace waterfall to find an error case.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will know how to explain distributed tracing and why it is essential for microservices debugging. You will be able to instrument applications using OpenTelemetry or OpenCensus so traces are generated and exported to Cloud Trace. You will analyze trace data in the Cloud Trace console to find latency bottlenecks and follow error propagation across services. Finally, you will correlate traces with logs and metrics and add custom spans and annotations to capture business context. Each objective includes a practical competency: instrument a small Python service to produce spans; filter traces by service or attribute; and enrich spans with attributes such as user or transaction IDs. These skills matter because tracing reduces mean time to resolution when incidents span multiple services, and because contextual attributes let you find the right trace quickly. You will practice hands-on steps and validation milestones that show you can both generate representative traces and interpret the waterfall diagrams that highlight problematic spans.

screens.title: What is Distributed Tracing?
screens.narratorSegment: Distributed tracing is an observability technique that tracks the end-to-end flow of a single request across a distributed system. At its heart, a trace represents that entire journey and is composed of multiple spans, where each span records a single operation's start time, end time, duration, and optional attributes. Imagine a user placing an order: the request goes from the frontend to an auth service, then to a product service, and finally to a payment service. A distributed trace ties all those calls together, revealing the sequence and timing. A concrete example: if payment calls are slow, the trace will show long spans in the payment service and shorter spans earlier in the chain, so you can see where time accumulates. A common misconception is that tracing replaces logs—traces complement logs and metrics. Logs provide detailed textual context; metrics show aggregated behavior; traces give per-request timelines. Another mistake is assuming traces always remain connected; without proper context propagation, traces fragment into disconnected pieces. Key takeaway: tracing turns cross-service uncertainty into a timeline you can inspect, filter, and act on. Ask yourself: which multi-service request in your system would you most like to visualize?

keyIdea.text: A trace is a request's full journey; spans are the timed operations within that trace, giving a hierarchical timeline.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.3 › What is Distributed Tracing?
Core Concept

Trace and Span Basics

A trace ties together spans that represent operations. Spans include names, duration, and attributes for context.

Example
User order: frontend → auth → product → payment. Each service creates spans forming a single trace.
Misconception
Tracing is not a replacement for logs; it complements logs and metrics to diagnose request-level issues.
Key takeaway
Traces convert cross-service sequences into a navigable timeline for each request.
Analogy
Think of a trace as a shipping manifest for a single package moving through different distribution centers. Each span is a handling step that records time and notes. When a package is delayed, the manifest shows exactly which center introduced the delay.
Check your understanding
  • What does a long span bar usually indicate? — Increased latency in that operation.
  • Why add attributes to a span? — To filter and find traces for specific users or transactions.

screens.title: Traces, Spans, and Hierarchy
screens.narratorSegment: A trace is made of spans arranged in a parent-child hierarchy. Each span represents a single operation—an HTTP request, a database query, or an internal computation. Spans record a name, start and end time, duration, and attributes which are key-value pairs that add context. The parent span typically represents a broader operation, while child spans break it into smaller steps. For example, a 'process_order' parent span may have child spans for 'validate_item', 'call_payment_service', and 'write_order_db'. This structure gives you two immediate benefits: first, you can see which sub-operations consume the most time; second, you can attach attributes at the span level to filter traces by business data like item id or user id. A common mistake is treating collection of spans as flat logs; preserving the parent-child links is how you reconstruct a full request timeline. Another contrast: spans are time-bounded, but logs are event records; use both together. Takeaway: design spans around meaningful, measurable operations so traces reveal the story of a request, not just isolated timing points. Traces, Spans, and Hierarchy means spans have a name, timing, and attributes; linked hierarchically, they reveal where time is spent inside a request.. In practical terms, how spans form a tree and what data each span contains. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.3 › Traces, Spans, and Hierarchy
Definition

Span hierarchy and attributes

Spans form a tree where each child span is a sub-operation of its parent. Attributes let you add business context used for filtering.

Span contents
Name, start/end, duration, attributes, status, and events.
Example tree
process_order → validate_item → call_payment_service → write_db.
Practical cards
Why hierarchy matters
It shows nested latencies and makes root cause analysis local to a span's subtree.
Misconception
Recording every micro-operation as a span can add overhead; focus on meaningful boundaries.
Key takeaway
Design spans to capture clear business or technical steps so traces are actionable.

screens.title: Trace Context Propagation
screens.narratorSegment: Trace context propagation is the mechanism that links spans across service boundaries so a single request remains a single trace. Typically, libraries propagate context using HTTP headers—common header formats include W3C's traceparent or vendor-specific headers. When service A calls service B, it sends the trace_id and parent span id so the downstream service creates a child span connected to the upstream span. A concrete example: Service A receives a user request, starts a parent span, and includes the trace headers on an outgoing HTTP request to Service B. Service B's instrumentation reads the headers and continues the trace by creating a child span. A frequent error is missing propagation through message queues or custom HTTP clients; if headers aren't forwarded, traces fragment into separate traces that can't be joined. Another mistake is double-instrumentation without proper context merging, which can create duplicated or noisy spans. Takeaway: ensure every communication layer—HTTP clients, message producers, and proxies—preserves trace headers so traces remain complete and meaningful. Trace Context Propagation means forward trace headers across all inter-service calls; without it, traces break into disconnected pieces.. In practical terms, how trace_id and span_id travel between services. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.3 › Trace Context Propagation
Process Flow

How trace headers travel

Trace IDs and parent span IDs must be propagated on each inter-service call so traces remain linked across services.

Service A
Starts parent span and sends trace headers on HTTP request.
→
Service B
Instrumentation reads headers and creates child span continued under the same trace.
Common mistake
HTTP clients or message producers that drop headers cause disconnected traces; explicitly forward headers across queues and proxies.
Pro tip
Use automatic instrumentation when possible so context propagation is handled for you, and validate propagation in a test environment.
Concrete example
Service A issues HTTP header traceparent: "trace-id...". Service B reads and continues the same trace, producing a single unified waterfall diagram that shows latencies across both services.
Key Takeaway

Always verify that every outgoing request preserves trace headers to keep traces intact.

screens.title: OpenTelemetry and Cloud Trace Integration
screens.narratorSegment: OpenTelemetry and OpenCensus are open-source frameworks that provide vendor-neutral instrumentation libraries for traces, metrics, and logs. To export traces to Cloud Trace you configure an exporter in your application. The exporter formats spans into the expected A P I model and sends them to Cloud Trace. The typical steps are: create a TracerProvider, attach a Cloud Trace exporter, and add a span processor to manage how spans are batched and exported. A concrete example is creating a TracerProvider in Python with a resource that names your service, then adding a CloudTraceSpanExporter so spans are sent to your project. A common misconception is that adding an exporter is enough; you also need to ensure your HTTP clients and other libraries are instrumented or wrapped so spans are created and propagation works. Another pitfall is forgetting credentials or project configuration; without a valid project ID and write permissions, spans won't arrive. Takeaway: instrumentation plus a correctly configured exporter and permissions result in spans flowing into Cloud Trace for analysis. OpenTelemetry and Cloud Trace Integration means set up a tracer provider, attach a cloud trace exporter, instrument frameworks or add manual spans, and verify spans arrive in the console.. In practical terms, vendor-agnostic sdks and how cloud trace receives spans. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.3 › OpenTelemetry and Cloud Trace
Architecture

How instrumentation reaches Cloud Trace

SDKs create spans and an exporter sends them to Cloud Trace. You configure a TracerProvider, exporter, and processors to control export behavior.

TracerProvider
Registers instrumentation and resources like service name.
Exporter
Transforms and sends spans to Cloud Trace using your project credentials.
Instrumentation
Automatic or manual; ensures spans are created for framework and library operations.
Concrete example
# Configure OpenTelemetry TracerProvider and Cloud Trace exporter
resource = Resource.create({"service.name": "my-python-service"})
provider = TracerProvider(resource=resource)
cloud_trace_exporter = CloudTraceSpanExporter(project_id="YOUR_PROJECT_ID")
provider.add_span_processor(SimpleSpanProcessor(cloud_trace_exporter))
trace.set_tracer_provider(provider)
This setup creates a provider, attaches the Cloud Trace exporter, and registers it so spans flow to Cloud Trace.

screens.title: Hands-on Python: Overview of the Example
screens.narratorSegment: The hands-on example in this chapter uses two small Python Flask services: Service A receives processing requests and calls Service B to validate items. Both services configure OpenTelemetry to export spans to Cloud Trace. Service A creates a span around the main processing logic and sets attributes like item id and validation status. It calls Service B over HTTP; automatic instrumentation propagates the trace context so Service B's spans appear as children in the same trace. Service B performs validation and returns a status attribute. When you run both services locally and send requests, Cloud Trace will show traces for both service-a and service-b. For an 'invalid' item, the trace will include an error span in Service B and a recorded exception in Service A. A common misconception is that you must instrument every dependency; in practice instrument the services you control and ensure propagation through the transport. The concrete outcome is a waterfall diagram that highlights the error and shows how latency is distributed across both services. Module 12 › Chapter 12.3 › service_a.py
Code excerpt
# app.py (simplified)
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import SimpleSpanProcessor
from opentelemetry.exporter.cloud_trace import CloudTraceSpanExporter
from opentelemetry.sdk.resources import Resource
from opentelemetry.instrumentation.flask import FlaskInstrumentor
from opentelemetry.instrumentation.requests import RequestsInstrumentor

resource = Resource.create({"service.name": "service-a"})
provider = TracerProvider(resource=resource)
cloud_trace_exporter = CloudTraceSpanExporter(project_id=os.environ.get("GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT"))
provider.add_span_processor(SimpleSpanProcessor(cloud_trace_exporter))
trace.set_tracer_provider(provider)

FlaskInstrumentor().instrument_app(app)
RequestsInstrumentor().instrument()

tracer = trace.get_tracer(__name__)

Module 12 › Chapter 12.3 › service_b.py
Code excerpt
# service_b.py (simplified)
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import SimpleSpanProcessor
from opentelemetry.exporter.cloud_trace import CloudTraceSpanExporter
from opentelemetry.sdk.resources import Resource
from opentelemetry.instrumentation.flask import FlaskInstrumentor

resource = Resource.create({"service.name": "service-b"})
provider = TracerProvider(resource=resource)
cloud_trace_exporter = CloudTraceSpanExporter(project_id=os.environ.get("GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT"))
provider.add_span_processor(SimpleSpanProcessor(cloud_trace_exporter))
trace.set_tracer_provider(provider)

app = Flask(__name__)
FlaskInstrumentor().instrument_app(app)

@ app.route('/validate/')
def validate_item(item_id):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("validate_item_logic") as span:
        span.set_attribute("item.id", item_id)
        # simulate validation
Explanation

Service B continues traces by reading propagated headers and creating spans for validation. Attributes on the span allow you to filter traces by item id or validation status in Cloud Trace.

Error case
If item_id is "invalid", the span sets validation.status to failed, which you will see in the waterfall and span details.
Takeaway
Downstream attributes are critical for diagnosing whether a business-level check failed in validation or earlier.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.3 › Correlate Traces, Logs, Metrics

Why correlate?

Traces show per-request timelines; logs contain detailed textual events; metrics reveal aggregated system behavior. Together they give complete observability.

Workflow
Detect via metrics → inspect representative traces → open logs using trace_id to get detailed context.
Concrete example
A spike in frontend latency leads you to traces showing a slow payment span; logs show a downstream timeout message for the payment API.
Best practices
  • Include trace_id in structured logs so you can link from a span to exact log entries.
  • Avoid extremely high-cardinality span attributes like raw user emails; prefer stable IDs.
  • Use sampling to control volume but increase sampling during incidents for deeper inspection.
Key Takeaway

Traces tell you where to look; logs tell you what happened; metrics tell you when and how often.

screens.title: Custom Spans, Annotations, Sampling, and Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Custom spans and annotations let you capture business-level context in traces, but they must be used thoughtfully. Create manual spans around important operations that automatic instrumentation may miss, and set attributes like user_id, item_id, or feature_flag_status to enable business-centric filtering. However, watch out for high-cardinality attributes—using unique identifiers such as emails or raw UUIDs on every span can make queries expensive and increase storage costs. Sampling is the mechanism to limit trace volume: configure a baseline sampling rate for production and increase it temporarily for incident debugging. A concrete trade-off: set sampling to one in a hundred for steady-state observability, but make specific endpoints always sampled when they represent critical transactions. Common mistakes include failing to propagate context across queues, over-instrumenting every small function, or failing to monitor trace data volume and sampling impact on costs. Takeaway: enrich traces where it yields diagnostic value, tune sampling for cost and coverage, and validate propagation across all communication paths. Custom spans and annotations

Use manual spans to capture key business operations and attach attributes that let you filter traces for those scenarios.

Good attributes
Stable IDs like user_id or item_id that help filter traces without excessive cardinality.
Avoid
High-cardinality values like raw emails or long text blobs on every span.

Sampling and pitfalls

Sampling reduces volume by tracing only a subset of requests. Choose a sensible default and increase sampling for incidents or critical endpoints.

Sampling example
1 in 100 steady-state, but always-sample payment transactions during a rollout.
Common mistake
Over-instrumentation creates noise and overhead; under-instrumentation leaves blind spots. Aim for balanced coverage around critical paths.

fullNarratorScript:
Distributed tracing gives you a single, end-to-end view of a user request that traverses many services. In practice, tracing helps you answer concrete operational questions: which service introduced latency, where did an error originate, and what path did a transaction follow? In this lesson you will learn the core trace concepts—trace, span, context propagation—how to instrument code using OpenTelemetry or OpenCensus, and how to use the Cloud Trace console to inspect waterfall diagrams and span attributes. We'll walk through a hands-on Python example with two small services that simulate a validation and processing flow. You will also learn how to enrich traces with custom spans and annotations and the trade-offs around sampling and attribute cardinality. As you watch, think about a scenario from your applications where a single user action touches multiple services. Tracing will help you connect that activity into one coherent story so you can locate bottlenecks and understand error propagation. At the end of this chapter you'll know what to instrument, how to read traces, and how to avoid common propagation mistakes.

By the end of this chapter you will know how to explain distributed tracing and why it is essential for microservices debugging. You will be able to instrument applications using OpenTelemetry or OpenCensus so traces are generated and exported to Cloud Trace. You will analyze trace data in the Cloud Trace console to find latency bottlenecks and follow error propagation across services. Finally, you will correlate traces with logs and metrics and add custom spans and annotations to capture business context. Each objective includes a practical competency: instrument a small Python service to produce spans; filter traces by service or attribute; and enrich spans with attributes such as user or transaction IDs. These skills matter because tracing reduces mean time to resolution when incidents span multiple services, and because contextual attributes let you find the right trace quickly. You will practice hands-on steps and validation milestones that show you can both generate representative traces and interpret the waterfall diagrams that highlight problematic spans.

This second objectives page focuses on practical skills you will exercise during the hands-on activity. First, configure OpenTelemetry SDKs to export to Cloud Trace and verify that spans appear in the console. Second, create custom spans for critical business logic so you can measure and filter those operations. Third, use the Cloud Trace console filters to find traces by service, attribute, or latency threshold. Fourth, practice correlating traces with log entries by ensuring trace context is added to logs. These competencies matter because instrumentation without analysis is noise, and analysis without context is guessing. For assessment, you will run two small Python services, generate traces for normal and failing requests, and answer targeted questions about waterfall diagrams and context propagation. Keep an eye on sampling settings and attribute cardinality during the exercise. The goal is not perfect coverage but clear, actionable traces for critical transactions.

Distributed tracing is an observability technique that tracks the end-to-end flow of a single request across a distributed system. At its heart, a trace represents that entire journey and is composed of multiple spans, where each span records a single operation's start time, end time, duration, and optional attributes. Imagine a user placing an order: the request goes from the frontend to an auth service, then to a product service, and finally to a payment service. A distributed trace ties all those calls together, revealing the sequence and timing. A concrete example: if payment calls are slow, the trace will show long spans in the payment service and shorter spans earlier in the chain, so you can see where time accumulates. A common misconception is that tracing replaces logs—traces complement logs and metrics. Logs provide detailed textual context; metrics show aggregated behavior; traces give per-request timelines. Another mistake is assuming traces always remain connected; without proper context propagation, traces fragment into disconnected pieces. Key takeaway: tracing turns cross-service uncertainty into a timeline you can inspect, filter, and act on. Ask yourself: which multi-service request in your system would you most like to visualize?

A trace is made of spans arranged in a parent-child hierarchy. Each span represents a single operation—an HTTP request, a database query, or an internal computation. Spans record a name, start and end time, duration, and attributes which are key-value pairs that add context. The parent span typically represents a broader operation, while child spans break it into smaller steps. For example, a 'process_order' parent span may have child spans for 'validate_item', 'call_payment_service', and 'write_order_db'. This structure gives you two immediate benefits: first, you can see which sub-operations consume the most time; second, you can attach attributes at the span level to filter traces by business data like item id or user id. A common mistake is treating collection of spans as flat logs; preserving the parent-child links is how you reconstruct a full request timeline. Another contrast: spans are time-bounded, but logs are event records; use both together. Takeaway: design spans around meaningful, measurable operations so traces reveal the story of a request, not just isolated timing points. Traces, Spans, and Hierarchy means spans have a name, timing, and attributes; linked hierarchically, they reveal where time is spent inside a request.. In practical terms, how spans form a tree and what data each span contains. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Trace context propagation is the mechanism that links spans across service boundaries so a single request remains a single trace. Typically, libraries propagate context using HTTP headers—common header formats include W3C's traceparent or vendor-specific headers. When service A calls service B, it sends the trace_id and parent span id so the downstream service creates a child span connected to the upstream span. A concrete example: Service A receives a user request, starts a parent span, and includes the trace headers on an outgoing HTTP request to Service B. Service B's instrumentation reads the headers and continues the trace by creating a child span. A frequent error is missing propagation through message queues or custom HTTP clients; if headers aren't forwarded, traces fragment into separate traces that can't be joined.
